note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once decided a real case following the view of Rabbi Eliezer: a woman who has gone three expected cycles without bleeding is not made impure retroactively when she bleeds again. Afterward he remembered that other Sages disagreed with Rabbi Eliezer, and he said: Rabbi Eliezer is worthy to rely upon in exigent circumstances. The Gemara then asks what it was that he remembered.
why: The Gemara is testing Rav Huna's view that a menstruating woman's retroactive impurity does not affect teruma. This case, which must have involved teruma, implies the majority view makes teruma impure retroactively, contradicting Rav Huna.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; ruled in this case according to Rabbi Eliezer and then reconsidered.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage whose lenient view Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi followed; other Sages disagreed with him.

terms.meaning: A situation of pressing need, when a minority opinion may be relied on even though the law normally follows the majority.
The rule that a woman who finds menstrual blood may be treated as having been ritually impure for a period before she noticed it, affecting pure foods she touched in that time.

flag: The last story segment continues into the Gemara's analysis of the case ("And we discussed it..."), which runs on past the end of the story.

note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi examined a woman's blood at night and declared it impure. Looking at it again by day, he declared it pure. He waited an hour and declared it impure again. Then he said: Woe is me! Perhaps I erred.
why: The Gemara is discussing how Sages examined blood and whether one may rule on it based on how it would have looked earlier; it questions his worry, citing a rule that one may not say the blood would have been impure had it been moist, and then rereads the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; examined the blood three times, changed his ruling twice and feared he had erred.

terms.meaning: A woman who found a stain could bring it to a Sage, who judged by its color whether it was menstrual blood making her ritually impure, or a color that leaves her pure.
Ritual status, not hygiene. A woman who is impure from menstruation may not have relations with her husband or touch certain sacred foods until she purifies herself.
